subject: money
topic: Richer countries did not get proportionally happier
angle: While some regions show a positive link between income and happiness, the relationship is not consistent worldwide and can even become negative in certain areas.
title: The Wealth and Happiness Gap

reveal.headline: Income and happiness do not always move together.
reveal.body: In some parts of the world, the relationship between wealth and well-being becomes negative. This means more money can lead to less happiness in specific regions.

explain.headline: The link depends on where you live.
explain.body: While rich countries are generally happier than poorer ones, the connection is not consistent everywhere. In Western Europe and Asia, the positive link is not significant.

matters.headline: Your environment shapes your progress.
matters.body: That may be why your personal success feels different than the national average. Your happiness might be tied more to local context than to your bank balance.

example.headline: The commute home.
example.body: You sit in a car in a wealthy city, looking at the lights. You have the money for the house, but the feeling of satisfaction is not there.

verdict: The evidence largely contradicts the proposed angle by showing that happiness often does rise with income, though this varies significantly by region.
caveat: The findings are inconsistent across different geographical regions and vary depending on whether the analysis focuses on absolute or relative income.
caption:
Wealth does not guarantee a specific level of happiness. 

Research shows that while richer countries are often happier than poorer ones, the link is not consistent worldwide. In some regions, the relationship can even become negative, and in others, it is not significant at all. The findings are mixed and vary by geography.
